exaggeration

/ig-zaj-uh-RAY-shun/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Exaggeration means a statement that represents something as larger, better, or worse than it really is.

Every fishing story Grandpa told ended in exaggeration: the trout barely longer than his hand grew, with each retelling, into a monster that nearly pulled him off the dock.

Worked Example

When Marcus said the cafeteria line was 'a thousand miles long,' everyone understood the exaggeration — the line was long, but it reached only to the salad bar.

An exaggeration represents one thing as larger, better, or worse than it really is. Marcus takes a single true detail — a long line — and inflates it far past the facts. It is a playful overstatement, not a whole comic performance.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

overstatement: Overstatement is a claim that goes past the facts — and it applies to statements only. Exaggeration is wider: a statement, a gesture, a drawing, or a lifelong habit can all exaggerate, representing something as larger, better, or worse than it is. Every overstatement is exaggeration in words; not every exaggeration is spoken.

hyperbole: Hyperbole is the literary device: deliberate, obvious overstatement chosen for effect — the name a glossary of literary terms would print. Exaggeration is the everyday word and needs no intent — it can be careless or unconscious. Grandpa's ever-growing fish is exaggeration; a songwriter's calculated 'rivers of sorrow' is hyperbole.

embellishment: An embellishment is an added flourish — an invented detail stitched on to make a story sound better than it was. Exaggeration inflates a detail that is already there, pushing a true thing past its real size. Embellishment adds what never happened; exaggeration overgrows what did.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

understatement: presenting something as smaller or less important than it is

accuracy: a description that matches the facts exactly

Where it sits · how far past the truth it goes — stretch → exaggeration → whopper

stretch vs. exaggeration: Calling a claim a stretch suggests mild inflation; an exaggeration plainly outgrows the facts.

whopper vs. exaggeration: A whopper is an exaggeration so enormous that nobody could mistake it for the truth.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — ex-

Prefix — ex-: 'out, up, thoroughly,' from Latin

Root — agger-

Root — agger-: 'heap, pile,' from Latin agger; the verb aggerare meant 'to pile up'

Suffix — -ation

Suffix — -ation: 'act or result of,' Latin noun-forming suffix

Put it together

Put it together: Put together, exaggeration means, at its roots, 'the act of heaping it up and out' — piling more onto a claim than the plain facts can support.

Where This Word Comes From

Where This Word Comes From: Exaggeration's root agger ('heap') does not survive as an English word of its own -- but agger was itself built from the Latin verb gerere, 'to carry,' and that verb is still hiding inside gesture, digest and suggest. So nothing in your vocabulary is built from agger, while the root behind it is everywhere.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Neutral; common in everyday speech, journalism, and test passages about advertising and argument.

Use exaggeration for a single claim or detail that outgrows the facts — a fish that gets bigger with each retelling, a wait called 'forever.' It can be playful, careless, or misleading, and it is not automatically funny. (A parody, by contrast, is a whole comic send-up of a work or style, and it often uses exaggeration as one of its tools — see this unit's word "parody".)
